(CNN)  -- Manny Pacquiao's two-round demolition of Ricky Hatton has set up the prospect of the biggest money-spinning fight in the history of boxing. Pacquiao lands a solid right to Hatton on his way to a comprehensive victory. The Filipino knocked out the plucky but outclassed Briton in Las Vegas on Saturday night -- earning him by a conservative estimate at least $2 million dollars per minute. Hatton, who could well now hang up his gloves, will pocket more than $8 million as a consolation. Pacquiao's all-action style is popular with boxing followers and in his native Philippines the theaters which screened his fight live with Hatton were sold out well in advance with a ferocious demand for tickets. But the really big money lies in the Pay Per View (PPV) revenues generated by the U.S. Home Box Office (HBO) network. USA Today reported Monday that early indications from cable companies were that the scheduled 12-round light-welterweight bout could get as many as two million buys. Co-promoter Bob Arum was delighted with the figures especially as initial estimates were suggesting about one million boxing fans would shell out their cash. "We know based on those early numbers and based on experience the event will perform extremely well. If I had to guess, anywhere between 1.6 million and two million homes, which is a home run," he said. The record for a PPV event is the 2.4 million buys for 'Golden Boy' Oscar De La Hoya's May 2007 fight with Floyd Mayweather Jr., which generated a staggering $134 million in revenue. Mayweather, who also beat Hatton in another 'superfight' at the back end of 2007, astutely chose Saturday night in Vegas to announce he was coming out of retirement. Mayweather, nicknamed 'money' because of the enormous revenues he generates, will face Mexico's Juan Manuel Marquez on July 18 in his return to the ring. But the talk of the boxing world is an eventual match up against Pacquiao with the notional pound for pound title at stake as well as a massive pay day. "If Mayweather wants a piece of the 'little Filipino', just be my guest," Arum said before the dust had barely settled on the Hatton fight. With the flamboyant De La Hoya retired after being handed a painful beating by Pacquiao at the back end of 2008, the mantle of PPV king is set to fall to one of the two men who ended his ring career. Despite the global recession, the appetite for top prize fighting remains strong, but it is the more flamboyant characters who draw the biggest audiences. Last November's HBO clash between former pound for pound champion Roy Jones Jr. and the brilliant undefeated Welsh world champion Joe Calzaghe drew less than 250,000 buys. The only potential obstacle to a Pacquiao-Mayweather bout, the dangerous Marquez aside, is the relative sizes of the two men. Mayweather is a natural welterweight and would want a fight at 147 pounds, with Pacquiao, who started his remarkable career at light-flyweight, wanting the match at a lower weight. But big business and money is set to talk and many predict the showdown will come late this year, almost certainly in Las Vegas.

**LAS VEGAS (CNN)** — Manny Pacquiao didn’t just cement his status as the best pound-for-pound fighter in the world on Saturday night—he redefined explosive power. 

In a chilling display of speed and precision, the Filipino icon knocked out Britain’s Ricky "The Hitman" Hatton in the second round at the MGM Grand Garden Arena, capturing the Ring Magazine junior welterweight title and sending a thunderous message to the rest of the boxing world.

From the opening bell, Pacquiao (49-3-2, 37 KOs) overwhelmed Hatton with blinding hand speed. He dropped the pride of Manchester twice in the first round, establishing complete dominance. The end came at 2:59 of the second round when Pacquiao unleashed a devastating left hook that landed flush on Hatton’s chin. 

Hatton fell flat onto his back, unconscious before he hit the canvas. Referee Kenny Bayless didn't bother to count, instantly waiving off the bout as medical personnel rushed to the ring. Hatton eventually sat up and was taken to a local hospital as a precaution, but the message had already been delivered: "Pac-Man" is a global juggernaut.

"I didn't expect this fight to be so easy, but I worked hard in training camp," Pacquiao said through a smile in his post-fight interview. "Nothing personal. I was just doing my job."

### A Box-Office Goldmine

The fight was not only a sporting triumph, but a monumental commercial success. 

Industry sources and HBO Pay-Per-View estimates indicate the event generated approximately **1.4 million PPV buys** in the United States, producing nearly **$78 million in domestic television revenue**. The fight also drew massive numbers in the United Kingdom, where hundreds of thousands of fans woke up in the early hours of the morning to watch their hometown hero.

The massive business translated to colossal paydays for both fighters. According to the Nevada State Athletic Commission, Pacquiao was guaranteed a base purse of **$12 million**, while Hatton was guaranteed **$8 million**. However, with the addition of pay-per-view revenues, international television rights, and a sold-out crowd of 16,300 producing a $9 million gate, both fighters are expected to pocket upwards of **$15 million to $20 million** each.

### The Elephant in the Room: Floyd Mayweather Jr.

While Pacquiao's victory party began in Las Vegas and stretched all the way to Manila, the combat sports world immediately turned its attention to what comes next. And all eyes are pointing toward one man: Floyd Mayweather Jr.

In a move that surprised few insiders, Mayweather announced his un-retirement just hours before Pacquiao stepped into the ring on Saturday, scheduling a comeback fight against Juan Manuel Marquez for later this fall. Mayweather's return sets the stage for what could be the biggest financially lucrative fight in combat sports history.

Adding fuel to the fire, Hatton was trained for Saturday’s bout by Floyd Mayweather Sr., who had engaged in a bitter war of words with Pacquiao’s Hall of Fame trainer, Freddie Roach, throughout the buildup to the fight. Roach’s masterclass game plan utterly dismantled the elder Mayweather’s defense-first philosophy.

"Floyd Mayweather Sr. said his son would beat Manny," Roach taunted during the post-fight press conference. "Well, if Floyd Jr. wants to fight, bring him on. Manny is ready for anyone."

Promoter Bob Arum of Top Rank was equally enthusiastic about a potential Pacquiao-Mayweather showdown.

"If Floyd beats Marquez, there is only one fight to make," Arum said. "It will be the biggest fight in the history of boxing."

For now, Pacquiao stands alone at the apex of the sport. Having started his career as a 106-pound flyweight, the 30-year-old senator-in-waiting from the Philippines has now won world titles in six different weight divisions. If Mayweather wants to reclaim his throne as boxing's king, he will have to go through a man who looks increasingly untouchable.

### **The New Pay-Per-View Powerhouse: How Pacquiao-Hatton Reshaped Boxing’s Economy and Paved the Way for a Megafight**

When Manny Pacquiao left Ricky Hatton unconscious on the canvas in the second round at the MGM Grand, he didn’t just cement his status as the pound-for-pound king of boxing. He officially declared himself the sport’s newest, most lucrative pay-per-view engine.

For years, the sweet science searched for a cash cow to fill the void left by Mike Tyson and the impending retirement of Oscar De La Hoya. With the financial success of Pacquiao vs. Hatton, combined with Floyd Mayweather Jr.’s impending return to the ring, boxing’s business model hasn’t just stabilized—it is on the precipice of an unprecedented financial boom.

---

### **Pacquiao vs. Hatton: A Global Financial Triumph**

The May 2009 clash between Pacquiao and Hatton was a masterclass in modern sports promotion. Generating roughly **850,000 to 900,000 domestic PPV buys** in the United States on HBO Pay-Per-View, the event pulled in over **$50 million in domestic PPV revenue alone**, supplemented by a sold-out MGM Grand Garden Arena gate of **$8.8 million**. 

While a 900k buy rate is impressive on its own, the true genius of the Pacquiao-Hatton event lay in its international cross-collateralization:

1. **The UK Factor:** Ricky Hatton brought the fiercely loyal British fanbase. In the United Kingdom, Sky Box Office reported over 1 million buys, an astounding figure that rivaled major domestic events in the US.
2. **The Asian Market:** Pacquiao’s godlike status in the Philippines, combined with surging interest across Asia, opened up closed-circuit and broadcast rights revenues rarely seen for sub-middleweight fighters.
3. **The Post-De La Hoya Validation:** Critics argued Pacquiao’s previous PPV success (his December 2008 stoppage of Oscar De La Hoya, which generated 1.25 million buys) was entirely driven by De La Hoya’s star power. Hatton proved Pacquiao could sell an event as the primary "A-side" attraction.

---

### **Measuring Up to the Gold Standard: De La Hoya vs. Mayweather (2007)**

To understand where Pacquiao-Hatton sits in the pantheon of boxing economics, one must compare it to the current benchmark: **Oscar De La Hoya vs. Floyd Mayweather Jr. in May 2007.**

| Metric | De La Hoya vs. Mayweather (2007) | Pacquiao vs. Hatton (2009) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **US PPV Buys** | **2.4 Million** (Record at the time) | **~850,000 - 900,000** |
| **US PPV Revenue** | **$136 Million** | **~$50 Million** |
| **Live Gate** | **$19 Million** | **$8.8 Million** |
| **Primary Economic Driver**| De La Hoya (Mainstream/Mexican Demographics) | Global Crossover (UK Fanbase + Asian Market) |

De La Hoya vs. Mayweather set the gold standard because it bridged the gap between hard-core fight fans and casual consumers, fueled heavily by HBO’s groundbreaking *24/7* reality series. De La Hoya was the established mainstream crossover star, while Mayweather played the villainous heir-apparent to perfection.

While Pacquiao-Hatton fell short of De La Hoya-Mayweather’s astronomical numbers, context is everything. Hits above the 800,000-buy threshold without De La Hoya on the marquee had become virtually extinct in the late 2000s. Pacquiao-Hatton proved that a compelling narrative (East Coast/West Coast of the globe, high-octane fighting styles) could still drive top-tier box office numbers in a struggling global economy.

---

### **The Financial Prospects of Pacquiao vs. Mayweather: A $200 Million Frontier**

With Hatton dispatched and Mayweather ending his brief "retirement" to fight Juan Manuel Marquez, the boxing world is fixated on the ultimate prize: **Manny Pacquiao vs. Floyd Mayweather Jr.**

From a pure business perspective, a Pacquiao-Mayweather fight is not just a boxing match; it is a mega-merger of two distinct, highly lucrative consumer markets.

#### **1. The Demographic Explosion**
* **Team Mayweather:** Draws the urban, high-roller, and "hate-watch" demographics. People pay either to see his technical brilliance or to watch him get knocked out.
* **Team Pacquiao:** Commands the global Asian demographic, mainstream sports fans who love his aggressive, fan-friendly style, and the casual Latino audience he cultivated by beating a legendary string of Mexican fighters (Morales, Barrera, Marquez).

#### **2. Financial Projections**
If promoted correctly, Pacquiao vs. Mayweather could shatter every record set by De La Hoya-Mayweather:
* **PPV Buys:** Conservatively projected to shatter the 2 million buy threshold, with a ceiling of **2.5 to 3 million buys**.
* **Gross Revenue:** With PPV prices likely to be pushed to a premium ($60–$70+), domestic PPV gross could easily surpass **$150 million**.
* **Live Gate:** Las Vegas casinos would enter a bidding war. The live gate could comfortably top **$20 million**, driven by high-net-worth foreign travelers and corporate sponsors.

#### **3. The Negotiation Minefield**
Despite the obvious pot of gold, the financial ecosystem surrounding this fight is fraught with friction:
* **The Purse Split:** Mayweather will demand a lion’s share (or at least a 50/50 split), viewing himself as the PPV king who defeated De La Hoya. Pacquiao’s promoter, Bob Arum (Top Rank), will argue that Manny’s recent pay-per-view tear and knockout spree make him equal—if not superior—value.
* **Promotional Rivalries:** The bitter blood between Golden Boy/Mayweather Promotions and Bob Arum’s Top Rank threatens to stall negotiations, as both sides fight over broadcast rights, venue control, and sponsor distribution.

---

### **The Verdict**

Pacquiao’s two-round destruction of Ricky Hatton did more than generate short-term revenue; it altered the economic landscape of combat sports. It established Pacquiao as an elite pay-per-view driver and set up the ultimate financial clash of this generation. 

If Floyd Mayweather and Manny Pacquiao can put pen to paper, they won't just be fighting for pound-for-pound supremacy—they will be participating in the highest-grossing single-day sporting event in human history. The ball is in their court, and the network executives are waiting with open checkbooks.

**SHOCKWAVE IN LAS VEGAS: Pacquiao’s Brutal Knockout of Hatton Ignites Demands for Mayweather Mega-Fight**

**LAS VEGAS —** It took less than six minutes for Manny Pacquiao to send a lightning bolt through the boxing world. Inside a roaring MGM Grand Garden Arena on Saturday night, the Filipino superstar delivered a terrifying, one-punch knockout of Ricky Hatton in the second round, capturing the Ring Magazine Junior Welterweight title and cementing his status as the undisputed pound-for-pound king of the sport.

The decisive blow—a blistering, perfectly timed left hook to Hatton’s chin—sent the Manchester native crashing flat onto his back, unconscious before he hit the canvas. Referee Kenny Bayless didn’t even bother to complete a count. As Hatton lay motionless for several tense minutes before eventually sitting up, Pacquiao fell to his knees in his corner, raising his hands in prayer.

The victory was Pacquiao’s third dramatic triumph in under fourteen months, following his brutal beatdown of Oscar De La Hoya in December 2008 and his split-decision victory over Juan Manuel Marquez in March 2008.

In the post-fight press conference, Pacquiao’s promoter, Top Rank CEO Bob Arum, could hardly contain his awe at what his fighter had accomplished.

"I’ve been in this business for over 40 years. I promoted Muhammad Ali, I promoted Sugar Ray Leonard, Marvin Hagler, Thomas Hearns," an elated Arum told reporters. "And I am telling you, I have never seen a fighter like Manny Pacquiao. What he did tonight to a great champion like Ricky Hatton was unimaginable. Manny isn't just a boxing star anymore; he is a global phenomenon."

Arum continued, emphasizing Pacquiao's transcendence beyond traditional boxing boundaries: "He hits with power in both hands that carries up through every weight division he enters. Nobody can prepare for that kind of speed and power combination. He is, without question, the greatest fighter I have ever worked with."

Yet, even as the confetti settled and Hatton was taken to a local hospital for precautionary scans, the boxing world’s collective gaze immediately shifted to a shadow that had been cast over Las Vegas all weekend: Floyd Mayweather Jr.

### The Shadow of "Pretty Boy"

Just hours before Pacquiao stepped into the ring on Saturday, Mayweather upstaged the fight-week atmosphere by holding a press conference at the MGM Grand to officially announce his return to the sport. Mayweather, who walked away from boxing in 2007 claiming he had nothing left to prove, announced he would end his 18-month retirement on July 18 to face reigning Lightweight champion Juan Manuel Marquez.

Mayweather’s tactical timing made his intentions clear: he was marking his territory. With Pacquiao’s devastating destruction of Hatton, a collision course between "Money" Mayweather and "Pac-Man" instantly became the only fight the public wanted to see. 

When asked about a potential showdown with Mayweather, Arum did not shy away, but he made it clear that Mayweather's upcoming fight with Marquez was a detour the sport had to endure first. "If Floyd beats Marquez, then we have the biggest fight in the history of boxing," Arum said. "Manny is ready for anybody. But Floyd has to handle his business first, and we'll see if he actually wants to step into the ring with Manny."

### The Weight Class Obstacles

Despite the overwhelming public clamor, making a Mayweather-Pacquiao fight is far from a simple negotiation. Beyond the intense personal animosity between Arum and Mayweather—who bitterly parted ways with Top Rank in 2006—the immediate roadblock to the mega-fight lies in the logistical nightmare of weight classes.

Pacquiao’s meteoric rise has defied traditional boxing physics. He began his career at 106 pounds and had just destroyed Hatton at the 140-pound Junior Welterweight limit. While Pacquiao proved his power carried to 140, his trainer, Freddie Roach, has expressed reservations about pushing his fighter permanently into higher weight classes where larger men could absorb his punches and bully him physically.

Mayweather, on the other hand, has operated as a full-fledged Welterweight (147 pounds) since 2006. For his comeback fight against Marquez, Mayweather insisted on a catchweight contract (initially set at 144 pounds), effectively forcing Marquez—a natural 135-pounder—to move up two weight divisions. 

If Pacquiao and Mayweather are to meet, the weight limit will be the primary battleground in negotiations:

1. **The Catchweight Dilemma:** Roach has stated he would prefer a Mayweather fight to take place at a catchweight of 143 or 144 pounds, ensuring Pacquiao does not give up a massive weight advantage on fight night. However, Mayweather historically disdains fighting below the 147-pound welterweight limit, viewing himself as the "A-side" draw who dictates terms.
2. **Size and Rehydration:** Mayweather walks around significantly heavier than Pacquiao. While Pacquiao weighed in at 138 pounds for Hatton and rehydrated to under 150, Mayweather routinely enters the ring as a robust 150+ pound welterweight. Pacquiao's team fears that fighting at a full 147 pounds gives Mayweather an unfair physical cushion.
3. **The Marquez Precedent:** Mayweather’s decision to fight Marquez at a higher weight class demonstrated his unwillingness to drain his own body to accommodate smaller opponents. If Mayweather refuses to yield a single pound below 147 for Pacquiao, Roach and Arum may hesitate to take the risk.

For now, the boxing universe remains in a state of hyper-anticipation. Pacquiao will return to the Philippines for a hero’s welcome and a well-deserved rest, while Mayweather prepares for his July clash with Marquez.

The victory over Hatton proved that Pacquiao is a generational force, capable of shutting the lights out on the world's elite in devastating fashion. But whether his blinding speed and newly discovered power can cross the weight-class divide to lure Floyd Mayweather Jr. into the ring remains the ultimate $100-million question.
